What affects the risk of chronic disease

An interactive map of the risk factors linked to heart disease, stroke, diabetes, dementia, kidney and lung disease and other major chronic conditions. Every link shows how strong the evidence is, including where studies disagree. Cancer has its own explorer.

For the curious public, clinicians, students and journalists.

Wenxin Wan works at IARC. He alone is responsible for the views expressed here, which do not necessarily represent the decisions, policy or views of IARC or WHO.

The map covers 45 diseases, 124 risk factors and 356 graded links. They come from 562 published sources, including GBD Burden of Proof, Lancet Commissions, pooled cohort consortia and published meta-analyses.

Before you read. This map shows whether a risk factor can cause a disease and how sure the evidence is. It cannot tell you how much a risk factor will affect you. That depends on your own baseline risk, the dose and how long you were exposed. A link here describes an average across whole populations. It does not tell you what caused any individual case, and many people with a given risk factor never develop the disease.

Explore the evidence

Start from a disease to see what raises and lowers its risk. Start from a risk factor to see everything it affects. Or open the network to see how they connect. The risk-factor list also includes things that lower risk, such as statins, the DASH diet and breastfeeding; their links are marked "Lowers risk" and drawn dashed on the map.

What the labels mean →
1 means no difference. Further right means higher risk, further left means lower risk. The scale is stretched so that half the risk and double the risk sit the same distance from 1.

    Chronic Disease Evidence Explorer

    A guide for the curious public, clinicians, students and journalists to the evidence linking modifiable risk factors to major chronic diseases. Every link records its effect estimate, exposure contrast, evidence grade and sources. Sister project to the Cancer Evidence Explorer, which covers IARC hazard identification.
